parts.label: a
parts.ask: A small ball is projected from \(O\) on horizontal ground with speed 28 m s⁻¹ at an angle \(\alpha\) to the ground. After \(T\) seconds it passes through \(A\), which is 40 m horizontally and 20 m vertically from \(O\) (Figure 2, with \(A\) on the way down). Modelling the ball as a particle moving freely under gravity, show that \(T = \dfrac{10}{7\cos\alpha}\).

steps.text: Horizontally there is no acceleration, so the speed stays \(28\cos\alpha\).

parts.label: b
parts.method: Vertical motion, taking up as positive

steps.head: Now use the identity for sec²

steps.why: Collect on the left, then divide by 10.

parts.label: c
parts.ask: Find the greatest possible height of the ball above the ground as it moves from \(O\) to \(A\).
parts.method: Solve the quadratic in tan α

steps.text: \(\tan\alpha = 1\) or \(\tan\alpha = 3\). Take the larger, \(\tan\alpha = 3\): the steeper path goes higher.
steps.why: With \(\tan\alpha = 1\) the top is only 20 m, at \(A\).

steps.head: Find sin α from a right-angled triangle

steps.text: Opposite 3, adjacent 1, so the hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{3^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{10}\).

steps.head: Vertical motion up to the top

steps.why: At the top the vertical velocity is zero.

parts.label: d
parts.ask: The model does not include air resistance. State one other limitation of the model.

steps.text: Air resistance is excluded, so name something else real that the model leaves out. One clear limitation is enough.
steps.why: Extra, wrong limitations can cost the mark.

parts.answerText: The model ignores the spin of the ball.

check.answers: a comment on the model: no number to compare
